To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
an aromatic residue switch in the σ-factor controls the activity of transcription initiation complexes.
an aromatic residue in the β-subunit of RNAP is a key switch in the formation of the functional open promoter complex.
an aromatic residue in the σ-factor of bacterial RNA polymerase acts as a switch that controls the transcription intermediate complex activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that aromatic residues in bacterial RNAPs play in controlling the formation of transcription intermediates and the transition between transcription intermediates and RPo.
understanding the role of the +1 tryptophan in transcription initiation.
the mechanism of RPi activity and how this is controlled by the σ-factor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tryptophan residue is a key player in the RPi to RPo transition, but the precise mechanism of its role remains to be determined.
the RPi activity is controlled by the aromatic residue at position 2.1 in RNAP and that this residue is involved in the RPi to RPo transition in the transcription of σ70-dependent promoters.
the tryptophan in question (i) is a critical determinant of the transcriptional activity of RPi complexes and (ii) is involved in the transition from RPi to RPO.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tryptophan residue is involved in the formation of the functional RPo by limiting the activity of at least the first intermediate complex (RP0) in a σ54-dependent manner.
we have shown that the tryptophan residue at position 100 in the σ-factor of the E. coli RNA polymerase (σ70) is important for transcription initiation.
the RPi activity is controlled by an aromatic residue switch in the RNAP catalytic centre.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aromatic residue switch is a general mechanism controlling transcription activity of the RPi.
a single aromatic residue in the σ-factor can be used to switch RPi activity in a promoter-specific manner.
a single tryptophane residue in RNAP can control the activity of a RPi by directly interacting with the flipped out DNA at +1.
